modules.title: Python Syntax Essentials
modules.intro: Python syntax interview questions are the first thing every fresher interview hits — before OOP, before frameworks, before any framework question. This page covers the Python data types every candidate should know cold (int, float, str, bool, NoneType, and the distinction between mutable and immutable), operators (arithmetic, comparison, logical, bitwise, the is vs == trap), control flow (if/elif/else, for loops, while loops, break/continue/pass), function definition (def, default arguments, *args and **kwargs at a concept level), variable scope (LEGB rule explained simply), and the string methods that come up in every fresher screen (split, join, strip, replace, format, f-strings). Every answer ends with what the interviewer is really asking — because fresher interviewers often phrase the same concept three different ways to see if you actually understand it or just memorised it.

modules.title: Python OOP Basics
modules.intro: Python OOP interview questions for freshers are about the four pillars — encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction — but interviewers want you to explain them in Python terms, not generic CS textbook terms. This page covers the class and object model (class as a blueprint, object as an instance), the __init__ constructor and the self parameter (why it's explicit in Python, not implicit like this in Java), encapsulation with single and double underscore conventions, single and multiple inheritance with method resolution order (MRO) explained simply, polymorphism through method overriding and duck typing, and abstract classes with the abc module. Every answer uses a short, complete Python snippet — a BankAccount class or an Animal hierarchy — not a Spring controller or a Java-style boilerplate dump.

modules.title: Python Built-in Data Structures
modules.intro: Python data structure interview questions for freshers almost always come down to one question the interviewer asks five different ways: 'do you know when to use each one?'. This page covers list (ordered, mutable, allows duplicates — the default workhorse), tuple (ordered, immutable — use when data should not change), dict (key-value pairs, O(1) lookup — the most important data structure in Python), and set (unordered, unique elements — use for membership tests and deduplication). It covers the comparison every interviewer asks (list vs tuple, dict vs set), list and dict comprehensions as the Pythonic way to build new collections from old ones, and the nested structure patterns that come up in JSON parsing. Every explanation starts with 'when would you reach for this one?' before the mechanics.

modules.title: Exception Handling & File I/O
modules.intro: Exception handling interview questions are a must for every fresher Python screen because they test whether you write defensive code or just happy-path code. This page covers the full try/except/else/finally block (what each clause does — the else runs only when no exception is raised, the finally always runs), Python's exception hierarchy (BaseException → Exception → specific exceptions), raising exceptions with raise, creating custom exception classes by inheriting from Exception, and the file I/O operations that almost always come paired with exception handling (open in read/write/append mode, the with statement as the safe way to close files automatically). Every answer explains what can go wrong, not just what the syntax is — because interviewers ask 'what happens if the file doesn't exist?' right after you give the syntax answer.

modules.title: Functions, Lambdas & Comprehensions
modules.intro: Python functions interview questions for freshers go beyond def and return — interviewers want to know if you understand how Python passes arguments, what *args and **kwargs actually do, and whether you can write Pythonic code instead of Java-with-Python-syntax. This page covers default argument values and the mutable default argument trap (the most common Python gotcha in fresher interviews), *args and **kwargs (how they capture positional and keyword arguments respectively), lambda as anonymous single-expression functions, map() and filter() as functional alternatives to for-loops, list/dict/set comprehensions as the idiomatic Python pattern for building new collections, and a first look at decorators at the concept level — what they do (wrap a function to add behaviour) without the full advanced decorator protocol.

modules.title: Data Structures & Algorithm Basics
modules.intro: Data structures and algorithm questions for Python freshers test whether you can think about efficiency, not just correctness. This page covers Big-O notation at the concept level (O(1), O(n), O(n²) — with Python list examples so the theory connects to code you already write), arrays and Python lists (how list operations like append and insert differ in complexity), the linked list concept (node + pointer, why it exists even though Python has list), stacks and queues (LIFO vs FIFO, how to implement both using Python list and collections.deque), basic recursion (how a recursive function calls itself, base case, the call stack — with factorial and fibonacci as examples), and hash tables (the dict under the hood, why O(1) lookup is not magic). These are concept-level questions at fresher interviews — you won't be asked to implement a red-black tree, but you will be asked 'why is dict lookup faster than list search?'

modules.title: Sorting, Searching & Common Patterns
modules.intro: Sorting and searching interview questions for Python freshers come up in two forms: theory questions ('explain bubble sort and its time complexity') and live coding questions ('find duplicates in a list'). This page covers bubble sort and insertion sort (the two sorts you must be able to code from memory and explain), the built-in sort() and sorted() with key functions (the Python way that you'd use in production), linear search and binary search (with the precondition for binary search — the list must be sorted — which is the first follow-up every interviewer asks), and the two simple problem-solving patterns that solve most fresher coding rounds: two pointers for sorted-array problems and the frequency-count pattern using a dict for string/array duplication problems. Each pattern comes with a worked example in 10–15 lines of runnable Python.

modules.title: SQL Fundamentals
modules.intro: SQL interview questions for freshers are asked at almost every Python backend interview regardless of experience level — because every backend developer eventually needs to write a query. This page covers SELECT with WHERE, ORDER BY, and LIMIT (the 80% of SQL you'll write every day), the JOIN types every interviewer probes (INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN — with a diagram-style explanation of what rows each one includes), GROUP BY with aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN — and the WHERE vs HAVING distinction that trips up most freshers), subqueries (when a SELECT result becomes the input to another SELECT), primary and foreign key constraints, and the index concept (why adding an index makes SELECT fast but INSERT slower — the trade-off question that separates candidates who understand databases from candidates who have only run queries). Every SQL example uses a simple two-table schema (orders and customers) so the join logic is clear.

modules.title: Python Database Basics
modules.intro: Python database connectivity interview questions for freshers connect the SQL knowledge you have to the Python code that executes it. This page covers the four steps every database operation follows in Python (connect → cursor → execute → fetch/commit → close), the sqlite3 standard library module as the no-setup-required starting point, the parameterised query pattern (%s or ? placeholders — the single most important concept in this module because it prevents SQL injection), why you must never use f-strings or string concatenation to build SQL queries (the SQL injection explanation that every interviewer loves to ask a follow-up about), psycopg2 as the PostgreSQL adapter and how its API mirrors sqlite3, and the ORM concept (SQLAlchemy or Django ORM as a Python-object layer above raw SQL — you don't need to be an ORM expert at fresher level, but you need to know it exists and why).

modules.title: HTTP & REST Basics
modules.intro: HTTP and REST interview questions appear in every Python backend fresher screen because APIs are what backend developers build. This page covers the HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE — and the idempotency distinction the interviewer always probes), the status code groups that matter for a backend developer (2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error — with the 200 vs 201 vs 204, 400 vs 401 vs 403 vs 404 comparisons that come up constantly), the request-response cycle (client sends request → server processes → server sends response — what travels in the header vs the body), JSON as the dominant API data format (how to parse it in Python with json.loads and json.dumps), the REST constraints (stateless, resource-based URLs, uniform interface — at the concept level), token-based authentication basics (why we send a token in the header, not a password), and the Python requests library for calling APIs from code.

modules.title: Flask Basics
modules.intro: Flask interview questions for freshers are about understanding the micro-framework philosophy — Flask gives you the minimum, and you build everything else. This page covers the Flask hello-world application (the five lines every interviewer asks you to explain), route definition with @app.route and URL variable rules (path parameters vs query strings), the request object (request.args for query params, request.json for request body, request.method), returning JSON responses with jsonify(), Flask's Blueprints as the way to split a growing app into logical modules, error handlers with @app.errorhandler, and the Flask vs Django comparison that every fresher interviewer asks: Flask is a micro-framework (routing + request handling, you add the rest), Django is a batteries-included framework (ORM, admin, auth, template engine all built in). Every code example is a complete runnable Flask application, not a snippet missing its imports.

modules.title: Django Basics
modules.intro: Django interview questions for freshers focus on the MTV architecture and the batteries-included features that make Django the most common framework name-dropped in entry-level Python JDs. This page covers the MTV pattern (Model-Template-View — how it maps to the MVC you learned in college, and why Django calls the controller a 'view'), the distinction between a Django project and a Django app (project = the whole site, app = a reusable component — this trips up almost every fresher), models and migrations (defining a model class, running makemigrations and migrate, why you need both commands), function-based views and URL patterns in urls.py, templates with the Django template language (context variables, if/for tags), the Django ORM at the basics level (Model.objects.all(), filter(), create(), get()), and the Django admin site (register a model, what you get for free, why it's a superpower for rapid development).

modules.title: Git & Version Control Basics
modules.intro: Git interview questions for freshers are asked at practically every Python developer interview because version control is table stakes — if you don't know Git, you can't be on a team. This page covers the three areas Git questions cluster into at fresher level: the daily workflow (init, add, commit, status, log, diff — what each command does and when), the branching model (why branches exist, how to create and switch with git branch and git checkout, what merge does, and why you get a conflict when two people edit the same line), and the remote workflow (clone, push, pull, fetch — and the difference between pull and fetch that interviewers love to ask). It also covers the merge vs rebase conceptual distinction (you don't need to know the rebase command cold, but you need to know that rebase rewrites history and merge preserves it), and the typical GitHub pull-request workflow that production teams use.

modules.title: Python Environment & Package Management
modules.intro: Python environment and packaging questions come up at fresher interviews more than candidates expect — because companies have been burned by 'it works on my machine' and dependency conflicts. This page covers why virtual environments exist (each project gets its own isolated copy of Python dependencies so project A's Django 3.2 doesn't break project B's Django 4.2), how to create and activate a venv (python -m venv .venv, source .venv/bin/activate, the cross-platform difference between Mac/Linux and Windows activation), pip install and pip freeze for capturing installed packages, the requirements.txt workflow (pip freeze > requirements.txt, pip install -r requirements.txt — the standard handoff between developers), pyproject.toml as the modern evolution of requirements.txt and setup.py (concept-level — you don't need to write it from memory), and environment variables as the correct place to store secrets and configuration (never in code, never committed to Git).

modules.title: Testing with pytest & unittest
modules.intro: Python testing interview questions for freshers focus on whether you understand why tests exist and whether you can write a simple one — not whether you've mastered pytest fixtures and parametrize. This page covers the testing vocabulary every fresher needs (unit test, integration test, the test pyramid at the concept level), the unittest module from the standard library (TestCase, test methods, setUp, tearDown, assert methods), pytest as the modern alternative (how it finds tests automatically, why assert statements feel simpler than unittest's assertX methods), the mocking concept (replacing a real database call or API call with a fake during tests — why you do this, what unittest.mock.MagicMock does at a basic level), test naming conventions (test_ prefix, descriptive names), and the question that separates candidates who actually write tests from those who just know the syntax: 'what would you test first for a function that validates a user email?'

modules.title: Behavioral & HR for Python Freshers
modules.intro: Behavioral and HR interview questions take up 30–50% of every fresher Python interview — not because the interviewer has run out of technical questions, but because at 0 YOE, your communication skills and attitude matter as much as your code. This page covers the questions that come up in almost every fresher round: the self-introduction (the four-part formula: education → project → skill highlight → why this company, in under 90 seconds), 'why Python?' (the answer that shows genuine interest, not 'because it's easy' which always lands badly), explaining a college project (how to frame it as a problem-solution-result story, not a feature list), strength and weakness (the framework for a genuine weakness that doesn't disqualify you), team conflict (the STAR answer structure for a disagree-and-commit story), career goals (realistic 3-year framing for a fresher), and the follow-up questions that come after every technical answer ('what would you do differently?' and 'how did you learn that?'). Every answer is written for a 22–24-year-old first-job interview, not a senior engineering manager behavioural.

modules.title: Python Type Hints Basics
modules.intro: Python type hints are expected even from fresher candidates at modern companies — mypy runs in CI and PRs that omit annotations often fail review. This module covers how to annotate variables and function return types, typing collections with List/Dict/Tuple or their lowercase equivalents (Python 3.9+), using Optional and Union (and the cleaner | syntax from 3.10), TypedDict and dataclass type safety, and running mypy on a small file to understand the error messages. Enough to write correctly-typed Python from day one and answer "why do we use type hints?" confidently.

modules.title: Calling External APIs with Python
modules.intro: Calling external APIs with the requests library is one of the most-tested fresher Python skills — nearly every take-home project and phone screen has you fetch data from a third-party service. This module covers the full workflow: making GET and POST requests, passing query params and auth headers, parsing the JSON response safely, handling non-200 status codes without crashing, setting timeouts so your script does not hang, reusing a Session for performance, and the retry pattern using urllib3 backoff. Small, practical, and directly applicable to any coding task or interview scenario.
